front: Define **work done** by a constant force.
back: $W = Fs\cos\theta$ — the force times the displacement in the direction of the force. Unit: joule (N m).

front: Give two situations where a force does **no work**.
back: When the force is perpendicular to the motion (e.g. tension in circular motion), or when nothing moves.

front: How do you find work done from a force–displacement graph?
back: Work done = **area under the graph**.

front: Kinetic energy formula?
back: $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$, or $\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$ in terms of momentum.

front: Change in gravitational potential energy near Earth?
back: $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$

front: Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring?
back: $E_H = \tfrac12 k(\Delta x)^2$ — the area under the force–extension line.

front: State the **principle of conservation of energy**.
back: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between forms; the total energy of an isolated system is constant.

front: Define **power**. Two formulas?
back: The rate of doing work: $P = \dfrac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}$, and $P = Fv$ for a force moving at velocity $v$.

front: Define **efficiency**.
back: $\eta = \dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}$ (energy or power). No unit; always below 1.

front: What does arrow width show on a **Sankey diagram**?
back: The amount of energy (or power) in that flow. Output widths add up to the input width.

front: Express the joule in SI base units.
back: 1 J = 1 N m = 1 kg m² s⁻².

front: When is the work done by a force negative?
back: When the force has a component **opposite** to the displacement ($90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$), e.g. friction or air resistance — it removes energy from the object.

front: A 50 N force pulls a sledge 10 m at 30° to the ground. Why is $W \neq 500$ J?
back: Only the component along the displacement does work: $W = 50 \times 10 \times \cos 30^\circ \approx 433$ J.

front: What is the **work–energy** relation?
back: The work done by the resultant force on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta E_k$.

front: A car doubles its speed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
back: It is multiplied by **4**, since $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$ depends on $v^2$.

front: When is $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ valid?
back: Only near a surface where $g$ is effectively constant (height changes small compared with the planet’s radius).

front: Hooke’s law and the unit of the spring constant?
back: $F = k\Delta x$ (within the elastic limit); $k$ in N m⁻¹. The area under the F–x line, $\tfrac12 k(\Delta x)^2$, is the elastic potential energy.

front: Speed of an object after falling from rest through height $h$ (no drag)?
back: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2gh}$ — independent of the mass.

front: When is total mechanical energy ($E_k + E_p$) conserved?
back: When only gravitational and elastic forces do work — no friction, drag or other dissipative forces.

front: Where does “wasted” energy usually end up?
back: As thermal (internal) energy of the surroundings, often via friction, drag or electrical resistance; it is spread out and hard to use again.

front: Unit of power in base units?
back: 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹ = 1 kg m² s⁻³.

front: A car moves at constant speed $v$ against total drag $F_d$. Output power of the engine?
back: At constant speed the driving force equals the drag, so $P = F_d v$.

front: A car is accelerating. Can you use $P = F_{\text{drag}}v$?
back: No. The driving force now exceeds the drag: $F = F_{\text{drag}} + ma$, and $P = Fv$ uses this driving force.

front: What does the gradient of an energy–time (or work–time) graph give?
back: The power.

front: You calculate an efficiency of 125 %. What went wrong?
back: Useful and total have almost certainly been swapped — efficiency is always below 100 % for a real device.

front: Energy changes of a swinging pendulum (no friction)?
back: $E_p$ max and $E_k = 0$ at the ends; $E_k$ max at the lowest point. $E_k + E_p$ stays constant.
